questionStem: A 42-year-old woman has the onset of chills 2 hours after transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells. She has a 1-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath with exertion; her hemoglobin concentration prior to the transfusion was 8.2 g/dL. Her temperature now is 38.5°C (101.3°F). The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration now is 10 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's fever?

choices.A: Bacterial contamination of the transfused blood
choices.C: HIV infection from the transfused blood
choices.E: Release of cytokines from the transfused blood

correctExplanation: Release of cytokines from the transfused blood is the most likely cause of this patient’s fever following the transfusion of packed red blood cells. Transfusion reactions are common and can range in severity from mild discomfort (eg, itching, fever, or mild rash) to life-threatening illness (eg, hemolysis or anaphylaxis). The time course of this patient’s fever (several hours after the start of the transfusion) and normal laboratory studies are consistent with an acute febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR), which is the most common type of transfusion reaction. FNHTR occurs because of the presence of preformed antibodies on donor leukocyte antigens and from cytokines in the plasma component of the transfused sample. It is typically mild in severity and resolves with supportive care. If symptoms occur during the transfusion, it should be paused to rule out ABO incompatibility. Antipyretics and consideration of other causes of fever are recommended. Recurrent FNHTR can be prevented through the transfusion of leukodepleted red blood cells.
incorrectExplanation: Bacterial contamination of the transfused blood (Choice A) is uncommon, but all potential causes of fever should be evaluated. Bacterial infection is more common after the transfusion of platelets. Bacterial infection as a cause of fever would generally occur later than 2 hours after the start of transfusion. Hemolytic transfusion reactions (Choice B) usually occur after clerical errors that result in the transfusion of ABO incompatible blood. In these instances, preformed antibodies against antigens on the surface of donor red blood cells leads to widespread hemolysis. This reaction is typically severe and may present with fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and occasionally death. HIV infection from the transfused blood (Choice C) is far less common in current clinical practice because of the universal screening of donated blood. Additionally, the symptoms of HIV infection would be delayed, and are unlikely to occur within 2 hours of administration of any contaminated blood products.

questionStem: Twelve hours after admission to the hospital for evaluation of a right lower quadrant abdominal mass, a 77-year-old woman has dyspnea. On admission, hemoglobin concentration was 6 g/dL. CT scan of the abdomen showed a 10-cm complex mass of the cecum. The stool was brown and tested positive for occult blood. She has received 3 units of packed red blood cells since admission. Pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Crackles are heard bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the cause of this patient's respiratory distress?
correctExplanation: An x-ray of the chest is most likely to confirm the cause of this patient’s respiratory distress. Most causes of acute dyspnea can be determined with a careful history, physical examination, chest x-ray, ECG, and blood gas analysis. In this case, the important history includes dyspnea that began after admission and following transfusion of three units of packed red blood cells. The physical examination discloses tachycardia, hypoxemia, and crackles on pulmonary auscultation. Given these findings, a chest x-ray will likely display pulmonary edema and vascular congestion associated with transfusion-induced hypervolemia, more commonly referred to as transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). In this syndrome, patients typically develop shortness of breath, tachycardia, and pulmonary edema within 6 hours of receiving a significant volume of blood products. Risk factors for TACO include renal dysfunction, heart disease, extremes of age, hypoalbuminemia, and a positive fluid balance prior to transfusion. Management includes discontinuing any current transfusions, placing the patient in an upright sitting position if tolerated, providing supplemental oxygen, and administering diuretics. Occasionally, positive pressure ventilation may be required in severe cases.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Arterial blood gas analysis (Choice A) is often useful in determining the cause of acute dyspnea, as it provides information on oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status. However, in this case, the history and physical examination findings are suggestive of a volume overloaded state, and a chest x-ray is more likely to confirm the diagnosis. Dipyridamole-thallium scan (Choice B) is used to evaluate myocardial perfusion in a non-exercise stress test. The temporal association between the patient’s symptoms and the recent transfusion argue against myocardial ischemia as the cause of the patient’s presentation.

questionStem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract for 4 hours. Three months ago, she was hospitalized for 20 days for treatment of necrotizing pancreatitis secondary to choledocholithiasis. Four weeks ago, she was admitted for a similar episode of bleeding. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with active bowel sounds. Endoscopy shows bleeding from gastric varices. The bleeding resolves with conservative treatment. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
correctExplanation: The patient’s presentation is most likely caused by splenic vein thrombosis resulting in variceal formation and subsequent upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The abdominal organs drain venous blood via both a systemic route (draining directly into the inferior vena cava) and the portal route (draining into the hepatic portal vein, then passing through the liver before entering the inferior vena cava). In the portal system, the inferior mesenteric veins and short gastric veins drain into the splenic vein, which then combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Thrombosis in the portal system in this region is a potential complication of pancreatitis due to perivenous inflammation as the splenic vein lies in anatomic proximity to the pancreas. Clinical manifestations depend on the location of the thrombus. For this patient, a thrombus in the splenic vein led to venous congestion in the draining gastric veins and formation of gastric varices. In addition to gastrointestinal bleeding, other complications of splenic vein thrombosis can include hypersplenism, thrombocytopenia, intestinal ischemia, and increased risk of abdominal infection.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Alcoholic hepatitis (Choice A) is characterized by jaundice, systemic inflammatory response (tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis), and increased serum concentrations of liver enzymes that occurs in the setting of heavy, chronic alcohol use. The patient may also have hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness. This patient does not have a reported history of alcohol use.

Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice B) is a risk factor for variceal formation due to portal hypertension. In this case, there is no additional history to suggest development of cirrhosis, and her recent episode of necrotizing pancreatitis supports a diagnosis of splenic vein thrombosis.

At the scene, his spine was immobilized with a cervical collar and backboard, and intravenous administration of fluids was begun. On arrival, he is alert. His temperature is 35.6°C (96°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 30/min, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 60 mm Hg. Examination shows angulation of the midthoracic spine. questionStem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He was an unrestrained driver and was ejected from the vehicle. On arrival, he is lethargic and confused. His blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg, pulse is 48/min, and respirations are 12/min. Physical examination shows flaccid paralysis of the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypotension?

Hypovolemia (Choice D) can lead to shock secondary to a reduction in intravascular volume, commonly related to hemorrhage or dehydration, which results in decreased cardiac preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output. questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of low back pain for 1 week and urinary incontinence for 2 days. He is currently undergoing chemotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with metastases to the liver. Examination shows tenderness to palpation over the lumbar spine and decreased sensation below the umbilicus. Rectal examination shows decreased sphincter tone. The prostate is diffusely enlarged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration

correctExplanation: A patient with a diffusely enlarged prostate likely has prostate cancer, which often metastasizes to the lumbar spine. An occasional declaring presentation of metastatic prostate cancer is low back pain, caused by metastasis to the lumbar spine. MRI of the spine is indicated for the evaluation of acute onset neurological deterioration. Cauda equina syndrome occurs from acute compression of the cauda equina nerve roots in the lumbosacral spinal canal, most commonly from an acute disc herniation or a traumatic or pathologic vertebral column fracture. This results in bilateral lower extremity weakness, loss of deep tendon reflexes, bowel or bladder dysfunction (eg, overflow urinary incontinence), and saddle anesthesia. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression.
incorrectExplanation:
Measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration (Choice A) is used as a tumor marker to monitor prostate cancer. While this patient likely has prostate cancer that has metastasized to bone, this patient's signs and symptoms of cauda equina syndrome are a surgical emergency and an MRI of the spine should be the next diagnostic step.

Urine culture (Choice B) is helpful in the diagnosis of urinary tract infections, which can present with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, and urgency. It would not cause spinal tenderness, numbness, or decreased sphincter tone, which is more indicative of a spine pathology.

Cystourethrography (Choice C) can be helpful in the diagnosis of urinary tract abnormalities, such as urethral stricture or urethral trauma, which can present with urinary retention. This patient's urinary incontinence is most likely due to spine pathology and less likely caused by a bladder or urethral anatomic abnormality.

questionStem: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department on a backboard with her neck and head restrained after a motor vehicle collision; she was not wearing a seat belt. She is awake but confused and has no memory of the crash. Examination shows a contusion on the right side of the head and clear fluid draining from the right ear. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.A: Comminuted skull fracture causing lymphatic disruption in the ear
choices.B: Cranial fracture that has disrupted the meninges
choices.C: Linear fracture of the temporomandibular joint
choices.D: Stellate fracture of the frontoparietal bone

correctExplanation: Basilar skull fractures typically occur after high-impact blunt head injuries, such as in this patient after a motor vehicle collision in which she was not wearing a seatbelt. A basilar skull fracture is defined as a fracture involving at least one of the bones that make up the base of the skull: the cribriform plate, orbital plate of the frontal bone, sphenoid bone, occipital bones, or the petrous or squamous portion of the temporal bone. In this patient with a contusion of the right side of her head and clear fluid draining from the right ear, a fracture of the temporal bone is likely. Patients with basilar skull fractures can present with hemotympanum, cerebrospinal fluid or bloody otorrhea or rhinorrhea, retroauricular and periorbital ecchymosis, and cranial nerve palsy. Cerebrospinal fluid leaks occur due to a meningeal tear of the dura, creating a communication that allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow out of the middle ear or nose.
incorrectExplanation: A comminuted skull fracture causing lymphatic disruption in the ear (Choice A) can result in a perilymphatic fistula, which is a fistula between the fluid-filled inner ear and the middle ear. A perilymphatic fistula can cause symptoms such as the sensation of ear fullness, hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and nausea. A linear fracture of the temporomandibular joint (Choice C), stellate fracture of the frontoparietal bone (Choice D), or zygomatic fracture (Choice E) would not explain the presence of clear fluid draining from the right ear, which is likely due to a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Linear skull fractures often are simple, closed, and have minimal clinical significance. The presence of external cerebrospinal fluid drainage is concerning for a basilar skull fracture.

questionStem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless large freckle on the back of her thigh that she first noticed 1 month ago. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. There is no personal or family history of skin lesions. She uses sunscreen with SPF 45 regularly. The patient is fair skinned. Examination shows a 1-cm lesion above the popliteal fossa. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Malignant melanoma is likely to be present when a lesion demonstrates asymmetry, irregular-appearing borders, variable coloration, a diameter greater than 6 mm, and rapid evolution in characteristics. It is a neoplasm of melanocytes, which contain pigment in melanosomes. Histologically, it may appear as dendritic cells containing pigment granules with high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios, mitotic figures, and increased size compared to normal melanocytes. Malignant melanoma can rapidly invade and metastasize, which carries a poor prognosis when diagnosed late. Subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, and acral lentiginous. Any lesion with features suggestive of malignant melanoma should be surgically excised with negative margins and pathologically examined for the depth of dermal invasion.
incorrectExplanation: Benign nevus (Choice A) is a common proliferation of melanocytes located in both the epidermis and dermis. They should not display asymmetry, border irregularity, multiple colors, or rapid evolution, as this would suggest melanoma. Keratoacanthoma (Choice B) is a cutaneous tumor characterized by a dome-shaped proliferation of keratinocytes with a central, keratin-filled crater. It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas. While most keratoacanthomas are characterized by a benign course, often undergoing spontaneous involution, some lesions progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Seborrheic keratosis (Choice D) is a benign proliferation of the epidermal keratinocytes. Lesions are typically round, elevated, brown, or tan in color, and sharply demarcated with a 'stuck-on' appearance. Solar lentigo (Choice E) is a benign pigmented macule that occurs on sun-exposed areas of the skin. It is uniform in color and does not change rapidly over time.

questionStem: A 65-year-old man comes for a follow-up examination 1 week after excision of a small raised lesion with pearly margins from the lateral left naris. The pathology confirms basal cell carcinoma with the tumor extending to the resection margin in one section. Examination shows a well-healed incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer and is derived from the basal cells of the epidermis. The primary risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is ultraviolet light exposure, though age, fair skin, and family history also contribute. Basal cell carcinomas typically present as pink, pearly papules or nodules with rolled borders and central ulceration most commonly on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include those that are less invasive, such as superficial and nodular, and those that are more invasive, such as infiltrative and morpheaform. In all subtypes, the risk of metastasis is low, though the tumors can invade locally and cause significant tissue damage. Biopsy may be performed with a variety of techniques, including excisional, shave, or punch biopsy. Treatment of basal cell carcinoma requires complete surgical removal, either via excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. In the case of incomplete excision, re-excision with negative biopsy margins is indicated to reduce the risk of metastasis.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Observation and reexamination in 6 months (Choice A) is inappropriate. Complete excision with negative margins is required for definitive treatment of basal cell carcinoma. Delay of repeat excision increases the likelihood of tumor recurrence and metastasis.

Laser therapy to the incision (Choice B) is incorrect. While electrodesiccation and curettage, as well as photodynamic therapy, are often used to treat basal cell carcinoma, laser therapy is not commonly employed and is inadequate in the setting of a prior excisional biopsy with a positive margin.

Radiation therapy to the nose (Choice C) is not necessary. Radiotherapy is typically reserved for older patients or those in which the anatomical location of the lesion renders complete surgical excision impossible. This patient would more greatly benefit from repeat excision.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining burns over 40% of his total body surface area in a house fire. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. The burned surface is anesthetic and covered with a thick, firm, brownish eschar; thrombosed vessels are visible through the burn surface. Over the next 24 hours, which of the following is the most urgent priority in management for this patient?
correctExplanation: Intravenous fluid resuscitation is the most urgent priority in management of this patient with a severe, full-thickness burn, which is often classified as a burn involving more than 20% of the total body surface area (TBSA) in adults. Severe burns can result in numerous complications, including compartment syndrome secondary to circumferential eschar formation, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy, and infection, but the priority within the first 24 hours is to replace the extensive fluid losses that occur during and immediately after a serious burn. The Parkland formula, which is calculated using the weight of the patient in kilograms and the percent of TBSA burned, is often used to calculate the estimated fluid requirements in the first 24 hours. Fifty percent of the total fluid requirements are given in the first 8 hours after the burn, and the rest is given over the next 16 hours. Ongoing fluid resuscitation following the first 24 hours is usually titrated to urine output, with a goal of 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/hr. Subsequent management should focus on providing temporary coverage of burned areas, ensuring adequate nutrition, managing pain, and treating or preventing complications such as compartment syndrome and infection.
incorrectExplanation: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice A) has not been shown to improve outcomes in burn victims in acute settings, although it is sometimes used later in the course for compromised skin grafts. The most common use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy is for the treatment of carbon monoxide poisoning and dive-related injuries such as decompression sickness. Administration of tetanus toxoid (Choice B) vaccine is important for all patients with any burn that is more than superficial if their tetanus vaccine status needs to be updated, but it is less critical than immediate fluid resuscitation in a severely burned patient. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (Choice D) as a prophylactic measure is not indicated in patients with severe burns. Although many of these patients may develop infections during their treatment and recovery, the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics in the absence of suspected or proven infection does not improve outcomes.

questionStem: A 47-year-old man comes to the emergency department 3 days after he sustained a painful injury to his right knee in a fall. He explains that he thought he had only scraped his knee but that the wound has been getting progressively worse. He has a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus well controlled with insulin. His most recent tetanus vaccination was 3 years ago. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 155/60 mm Hg. A photograph of the right knee is shown. Palpation of the affected knee produces pain and crepitation. An x-ray of the right knee shows gas in the soft tissue and no bony abnormalities. Analgesic therapy is begun, and urgent surgical debridement is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Antibiotic therapy is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient with evidence of necrotizing fasciitis, an infection typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, although singular organisms such as Clostridium perfringens or Staphylococcus aureus are sometimes encountered. Necrotizing fasciitis refers to infection spreading along a deep fascial plane that presents with acute onset of pain out of proportion to examination findings, erythema, and paresthesia, which progresses to anesthesia, typically occurring at a site of prior trauma or surgery. Risk factors include trauma and underlying chronic systemic illnesses, such as diabetes mellitus, liver failure, or renal failure. As the bacterial infection spreads along the deep fascial planes, bullae with or without crepitus may develop. The extent of infection is often difficult to assess by examination alone, although x-rays may disclose the presence of gas in the soft tissues. Treatment requires broad spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and emergent debridement of the infected tissue. Often, multiple sequential debridements for definitive management are required. Empiric antibiotics usually include vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, or meropenem. In this patient, antibiotic therapy should be initiated immediately. Surgical debridement is planned, but antibiotics should be started as soon as possible.

questionStem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling in his right leg. He reports that the pain started suddenly and is out of proportion to the examination findings. On physical examination, there is erythema, swelling, and tenderness over the right thigh. There is also a small area of skin necrosis with bullae formation. The patient has a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 24/min. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 22,000/mm³. An x-ray of the leg shows gas in the soft tissues. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Antibiotic therapy is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient with evidence of necrotizing fasciitis, an infection typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, although singular organisms such as Clostridium perfringens or Staphylococcus aureus are sometimes encountered. Treatment requires broad spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and emergent debridement of the infected tissue. Often, multiple sequential debridements for definitive management are required. Empiric antibiotics usually include vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam for broad coverage in addition to clindamycin to inhibit toxin production in cases of monomicrobial infection with Clostridium perfringens or Streptococcus pyogenes.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F. MRI of the knee (Choice A) is unnecessary and will lead to a delay in treatment for this patient. Necrotizing fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and does not require any imaging prior to surgical intervention and antibiotic therapy. Application of silver sulfadiazine (Choice B) is used for the treatment of burns and would not be helpful for this patient with a severe necrotizing infection. Early administration of intravenous antibiotics is paramount.

questionStem: A previously healthy 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after sustaining an injury to her upper arm while playing ice hockey. Examination shows diffuse swelling over the upper arm; the skin is intact. There is absence of wrist extension. X-rays show a fracture of the distal humerus. Which of the following is the most likely site of nerve injury?
correctExplanation: The radial nerve courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. It is often injured in displaced midshaft or distal humerus fractures, with resulting wrist drop. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles within the posterior compartment of the forearm, and sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. It does not innervate the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Injury to the nerve at the mid-diaphyseal or distal humerus causes extensor muscle function loss at the hand and fingers, weakness of supination, the presence of wrist drop, and sensory loss over the dorsal forearm, dorsal hand, and dorsal thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, F, G, and H.

A proximal humerus injury, such as a surgical neck fracture, can lead to axillary nerve injury (Choice A), which would result in dysfunction of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the proximal lateral arm.

Median nerve injury (Choices B and C) presents with weakness involving the flexor compartment of the forearm, thenar eminence, and first two lumbrical muscles, along with diminished sensation over the volar forearm and lateral hand. This patient presents with absence of wrist extension, which is caused by a radial nerve injury.

questionStem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He was an unrestrained driver in a head-on collision and sustained multiple injuries, including a right humeral midshaft fracture. On physical examination, he is unable to extend his right wrist. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?

choices.E: Radial nerve at the midshaft of the humerus

correctExplanation: The radial nerve courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. This patient presents with absence of wrist extension, which is caused by a radial nerve injury. The musculocutaneous nerve (Choice D) controls motor function of the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, along with sensory innervation over the lateral forearm. Injury would result in impaired forearm flexion. A distal humerus fracture would cause radial nerve injury above, not at the elbow (Choice F). The ulnar nerve (Choices G and H) supplies motor fibers to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensation over the anteromedial ring and small fingers and medial palm. Damage to the roots or to the nerve along its course (eg, in the cubital tunnel) can result in motor dysfunction of the fingers, and numbness or paresthesia involving the medial aspect of the upper extremity.

questionStem: An 82-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit after undergoing an uncomplicated, elective sigmoid colectomy for chronic diverticulitis. He is extubated and rates his pain as a 2 on a 10-point scale. He has a history of coronary artery disease. His medications are atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. There is jugular venous distention. Expiratory wheezes are heard at both lung bases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient is displaying classic signs of acute congestive heart failure. These include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, jugular venous distension, and end-expiratory pulmonary wheezes (sometimes referred to as a cardiac wheeze because of the association with pulmonary edema resulting from heart failure). Other signs of congestive heart failure can include shortness of breath, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and production of frothy sputum in left-sided failure, while right-sided failure is characterized by an increased jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral extremity edema. Anesthesia and surgery place significant stress on the body, and myocardial demand can exceed cardiac output, especially in an older patient with underlying coronary artery disease. Additionally, surgeries complicated by blood loss and fluid shifting may result in the need for administration of several liters of crystalloid or blood product to maintain hemodynamic stability. Treatment of an acute exacerbation of congestive heart failure consists of diuresis and respiratory support (eg, supplemental oxygen, positive pressure ventilation), and in more severe cases, intravenous positive inotropes and a ventricular assist device may be needed if cardiogenic shock is occurring.
incorrectExplanation: Cor pulmonale (Choice B) describes right ventricular failure resulting from chronic pulmonary hypertension. Left ventricular contractility and afterload are not affected. The patient is not displaying signs of right heart failure. Myocardial infarction (Choice C) can result in acute congestive heart failure if a large ventricular territory is affected; however, patients typically present with dyspnea and angina that is relieved by rest and nitroglycerin. While this patient does have a history of coronary artery disease, there is no additional evidence that his acute heart failure is caused by a myocardial infarction.

questionStem: A 30-year-old woman has had frequent palpitations and dyspnea with mild exertion for 2 days. She underwent an aortic valve replacement for rheumatic heart disease 2 years ago. She is receiving warfarin therapy. Her pulse is 80/min and regular, and blood pressure is 140/palpable mm Hg. She has pale conjunctiva. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Prosthetic heart sounds and loud systolic and diastolic murmurs are heard. There is trace edema of the lower extremities. Hematocrit is 24% with numerous schistocytes and fractured erythrocytes. Leukocyte count is 14,000/mm³. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly without redistribution of blood flow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: This patient’s presentation is most concerning for dysfunction of the prosthetic valve. There is a large difference between her systolic and diastolic blood pressures (increased pulse pressure), which is best explained by significant aortic insufficiency. This is further supported by the presence of diastolic murmurs and trace peripheral edema. During exertion, the backflow of blood results in cardiac output that is unable to match metabolic demands, accounting for her dyspnea. The presence of anemia and schistocytes is suggestive of valve-related hemolysis, which is a complication of prosthetic valves often caused by a structurally degraded, mispositioned, or leaking valve.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Cor pulmonale (Choice A) describes right ventricular failure resulting from chronic pulmonary hypertension. This patient does not have prominent evidence of right heart failure or pulmonary pathology.

Pulmonary emboli (Choice C) typically present with pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. It would be unusual for a patient taking a therapeutic dose of warfarin for a prosthetic heart valve to have a pulmonary embolism, though break-through emboli can occur. An embolus would not explain the patient’s murmur or schistocytes.

Ruptured papillary muscle (Choice D) is an uncommon complication of myocardial infarction and infective endocarditis. It results in severe mitral valve regurgitation and cardiogenic shock. The severity of the presentation is not consistent with a ruptured papillary muscle.

questionStem: One day after undergoing open cholecystectomy, a 47-year-old woman has increased blood pressure and moderate abdominal pain. She was not taking any medications prior to the operation. Postoperatively, she has been receiving lactated Ringer solution (125 mL/h) and patient-controlled morphine with a bolus dose of 1 mg and a maximum dose of 6 mg/h; there is a 10-minute lockout interval and no basal rate. She has been given nothing orally. She is alert and cooperative. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 22/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 170/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. There is no jugular venous distention or edema. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft with moderate tenderness; movement produces pain. Bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's hypertension?

choices.B: Increase rate of lactated Ringer solution

correctExplanation: Appropriate pain control is important in preventing postoperative complications. This patient has abdominal pain associated with hypertension, tachycardia, and respiratory splinting (eg, shallow breaths due to pain), the latter of which puts her at increased risk for atelectasis and consequent pneumonia. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is a frequently used option for controlling postoperative pain with opioid analgesics, such as morphine, hydromorphone, and fentanyl. Typical PCA set-ups include a basal rate, a bolus dose with a lockout interval, and a total hourly limit. Benefits of PCA use include improved patient satisfaction, titratability, and decreased risk for sedation given the frequent, smaller boluses, as compared to larger bolus doses that would be given less frequently by nursing staff. However, PCAs are associated with an overall increase in opioid usage. Basal rates are rarely used, as they can be associated with increased respiratory depression and overdose; therefore, they are often reserved for opioid tolerant patients. Thus, in this patient with signs of uncontrolled postoperative pain, her bolus of morphine should be increased.
incorrectExplanation: Increasing the rate of lactated Ringer solution (Choice B) is not necessary, as this patient does not demonstrate signs of hypovolemia and is already receiving adequate maintenance fluids. This patient has an appropriate blood pressure, and her tachycardia is more likely secondary to uncontrolled pain, rather than hypovolemia. Intravenous furosemide therapy (Choice C) is not indicated in this patient. She demonstrates no signs of volume overload, such as jugular venous distention or peripheral edema.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He feels well. He has hypertension well controlled with enalapril. Five years ago, he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years but stopped smoking 20 years ago. He walks 1 mile daily. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows a nontender pulsatile mass in the mid abdomen; no bruits are heard. Femoral pulses are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a 4-cm aneurysm; there is no evidence of rupture. Which of the following factors provides the best rationale for serial imaging rather than surgical repair in this patient?

choices.C: The patient's history of cardiac disease

correctExplanation: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) refers to a dilation of the abdominal aorta (> 3 cm), most commonly occurring inferior to the take-off of the renal arteries. It is often asymptomatic, although it can present with abdominal pain or hemodynamic instability if rupture has occurred. Physical examination may disclose a pulsatile abdominal mass, as in this patient, but it can also be unremarkable. Diagnosis is made with abdominal ultrasonography or CT scan. Risk factors for the development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm include advanced age, male sex, a smoking history, vascular disease, and connective tissue diseases, whereas the risk factors for rupture include current smoking, hypertension, and, most importantly, a large aneurysm size (> 5.5 cm) or rapid enlargement (> 0.5 cm over 6 months). When the risk of rupture is high, surgical repair is often recommended; if the risk of rupture is low, serial imaging is appropriate. Therefore, given this patient’s history, it is most appropriate for him to undergo serial imaging, rather than surgical repair, given the size of his aneurysm.
incorrectExplanation: Absence of symptoms (Choice A) is not often used in the decision process regarding the need for surgical repair of AAA. While symptoms may cause an aneurysm to be repaired sooner, large (> 5.5 cm) or rapidly enlarging (> 0.5 cm over 6months) aneurysms, even if asymptomatic, should be surgically repaired due to the high risk of rupture and consequent mortality. Age of the patient (Choice B) is not a factor that is used to decide whether an AAA should undergo surgical repair or serial imaging. Patients at the extremes of age may be too frail to undergo surgical repair, and serial imaging may be more appropriate; however, age alone is not a sole factor used to determine appropriate management.

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up appointment. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He is a former smoker with a 30-pack-year smoking history. He has no current symptoms. His blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 80/min. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile abdominal mass. An abdominal ultrasound shows a 5.8-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Patients at the extremes of age may be too frail to undergo surgical repair, and serial imaging may be more appropriate; however, age alone is not a sole factor used to determine appropriate management. The patient's history of cardiac disease (Choice C) and the patient's history of hypertension (Choice D) put him at increased risk for the development of an AAA. However, the risk of rupture is more closely related to ongoing hypertension and aneurysmal size. This patient's blood pressure is currently well-controlled, making the size of his aneurysm a more important aspect in determining whether to closely follow his aneurysm or surgically repair it.

questionStem: A 30-year-old male firefighter has been hospitalized for 3 weeks for treatment of third-degree burns involving the neck, upper anterior chest, and right upper extremity. A purulent exudate is noted at an intravenous catheter site located in the proximal cephalic vein just above the left wrist. When the catheter is removed, additional purulent exudate drains from the site. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows an 8-cm segment of the cephalic vein that is firm, tender, indurated, erythematous, and fluctuant. In addition to intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Application of a negative pressure dressing
choices.B: Elevation of the left arm and application of warm compresses
choices.E: Intravenous administration of tissue plasminogen activator

correctExplanation: Catheter-related bloodstream infections are a common cause of fever in hospitalized patients and can be complicated by catheter-associated septic thrombophlebitis. The infected thrombus serves as a nidus for microbial proliferation and presents with fever and signs and symptoms of bacteremia. The involved vein may display erythema and induration and there may be purulent drainage from the catheter site. The diagnosis may be aided by duplex ultrasonography or with contrasted CT scan. Treatment of catheter-associated septic thrombophlebitis includes infectious source control with removal of the catheter and surgical excision of the affected vein. Intravenous antibiotics should be continued and adjusted to microbial sensitivities, when possible.
incorrectExplanation: Application of a negative pressure dressing (Choice A) is useful in the management of a variety of wounds, including burns, pressure ulcers, and diabetic foot wounds. Their use is often contraindicated in the setting of ongoing wound infection. Additionally, a negative pressure dressing will not provide adequate source control without first removing the catheter and excising the affected vein. Elevation of the left arm and application of warm compresses (Choice B) is inadequate for providing source control of the infected venous thrombus. Intravenous administration of anticoagulants such as heparin (Choice D) or tissue plasminogen activator (Choice E) does not have well-established benefits in the setting of septic thrombophlebitis and is not recommended for most patients.

questionStem: A 65-year-old man is hospitalized for treatment of a urinary tract infection. He has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On the third day of hospitalization, he develops fever and chills. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 20/min. Physical examination shows erythema and induration over the left antecubital fossa, where a peripheral intravenous catheter was placed 2 days ago. There is purulent drainage at the catheter site. questionStem: A 58-year-old woman has had pain and tenderness of the long bones of the lower extremities, knees, and ankles for 2 months. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. She was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung 6 months ago. She has had rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years. She fractured her ankle in a fall 6 years ago. Examination of the lower extremities shows tenderness to palpation of the femur and tibia bilaterally and slight warmth and tenderness of the knees and ankles. X-rays show periosteal new bone formation of the femurs. Her symptoms are most likely a complication of which of the following?

choices.E: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

correctExplanation: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is often complicated by hypercalcemia caused by paraneoplastic parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) production. This protein acts similarly to parathyroid hormone (PTH), causing an increase in osteoclast activity via G protein coupled receptors. It also causes increased absorption of calcium in the intestine and renal tubules. Bone pain is a common manifestation. Other symptoms include abdominal discomfort, muscle pain and weakness, polyuria, and psychiatric disturbances. Hypercalcemia is also associated with hypophosphatemia, subperiosteal bone resorption, nephrolithiasis, and renal failure. Management is determined by the severity of calcium imbalance and symptoms. Asymptomatic cases are treated with oral fluid intake and reduced dietary calcium, while severe cases require hospitalization, intravenous fluid administration, and medications that inhibit bone resorption (typically bisphosphonates).
incorrectExplanation: Osteoporosis (Choice A) is a condition of low bone mass typically occurring in postmenopausal female patients. Its prevalence increases with age and, as a result, most guidelines recommend screening for osteoporosis after age 65 years. It is often asymptomatic until a traumatic injury results in a fracture, most commonly involving the hip, distal radius, or vertebrae. The history of prior trauma to the ankle (Choice C) is associated with a fall and not suggestive of osteoporosis. Though treatment and prevention of osteoporosis involve oral calcium and vitamin D repletion, hypercalcemia would be an unusual complication of the low supplemental dosages. Primary hyperparathyroidism (Choice B) should be considered in a patient presenting with symptoms of hypercalcemia. Causes of hypercalcemia can be categorized as either PTH-dependent or PTH-independent. In a patient with known squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, PTHrP secretion is a more likely diagnosis.

questionStem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressive fatigue and weight loss over the last 3 months. She also reports occasional abdominal discomfort and constipation. She has a 40-pack-year smoking history. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. Physical examination shows mild muscle weakness. Laboratory results reveal hypercalcemia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

choices.E: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

questionStem: Six days after abdominoperineal resection of the rectum for cancer, a 62-year-old woman becomes dyspneic as she walks to the bathroom. The postoperative course had been uncomplicated. PE is the more likely cause of this patient’s tachypnea, tachycardia, and dyspnea.

Congestive heart failure (Choice B) is unlikely in this patient with no cardiac history. While congestive heart failure can cause dyspnea, it is often associated with peripheral edema, increased jugular venous distention, and crackles on pulmonary auscultation, none of which this patient exhibits.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision; he was not wearing a seat belt and struck his chest on the dashboard. Examination shows a fracture of the right arm; an x-ray of the chest shows minimal haziness in the right midlung field. Forty-eight hours later, he has a cough, and crackles are heard on auscultation. He is afebrile. A repeat x-ray shows confluent infiltrates over the left and right upper lobes. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary contusions may occur after blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest. They often underlie the region of trauma to the chest wall and result from damage to capillaries with associated leakage of fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveolar spaces. This can result in hypoxemia if it involves and compromises a large enough region of the lung. On chest x-rays, pulmonary contusions appear as interstitial infiltrates and/or patchy alveolar opacities. The extent and distribution depend on the mechanism, location, and force of trauma to the chest wall. Management of pulmonary contusions is supportive with control of pain, pulmonary toilet, lung expansion, and maintenance of adequate ventilation/oxygenation of the patient.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Anaerobic pneumonitis (Choice A) refers to an acute irritant injury of the pulmonary alveoli and airways caused by inhalation of gastric contents. It presents similarly to aspiration pneumonia with pain, shortness of breath and cough, but is distinguished from aspiration pneumonia by lack of fever, though there is substantial clinical overlap in the presentations. Radiographic appearance is variable and may range from ground glass opacity to focal consolidation.

Aspiration pneumonia (Choice B) is characterized by fever, cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, malaise, and chest discomfort following an aspiration event. Frequently, aspiration occurs in a dependent segment of the lung, such as bilateral lower lobes when erect, or the lingula, right middle lobe, and superior segments of the lower lobes while prone or supine. Focal consolidation is typically visible on x-ray.

Fat embolism (Choice C) typically occurs acutely following a long bone fracture with resultant fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, petechiae, and conjunctival hemorrhage.

questionStem: An obese 37-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. He was the restrained front-seat passenger. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Ecchymoses are visible over the midabdomen from the lap belt. A nasogastric tube is inserted. An x-ray of the chest shows an obscured left hemidiaphragm with the tip of the nasogastric tube in the lower left side of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture can occur after blunt trauma that causes a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure and leads to rupture of the diaphragm. An opening in the diaphragm can lead to the herniation of abdominal contents into the thorax, and often presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and bowel sounds within the expected lung fields. It most commonly occurs in the left hemithorax and may be visualized as intestinal loops or other abdominal organs in the thorax on x-ray. In this patient, the presence of the nasogastric tube in the lower left side of the chest raises suspicion for diaphragmatic rupture. Management includes surgical exploration and repair of the ruptured diaphragm.
incorrectExplanation:
An esophageal rupture (Choice B) permits translocation of gastrointestinal contents such as food, stomach acid, and bacteria into the mediastinum, which if untreated, can lead to mediastinitis. Mediastinitis can present with chest pain, fever, and moribund appearance; the examination may disclose crepitus over the chest wall or neck, and a crunching sound may be heard on auscultation.

Pancreatic injury (Choice C) can present with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, and if severe, persistent hypotension. It would not explain the presence of the nasogastric tube in the lower left side of the chest.

It often underlies the region of trauma to the chest wall and results from damage to capillaries with associated leakage of intravascular and extravascular fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveolar airspaces, respectively. questionStem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with a history of alcohol use disorder, fever, abdominal pain, and ascitic fluid containing numerous neutrophils. SBP refers to the development of a peritoneal infection in patients with ascites that is not caused by instrumentation or introduction of bacteria into the peritoneum from an alternative source. This patient most likely has cirrhosis from chronic alcohol use. SBP is a common complication in patients with cirrhosis and ascites, regardless of the etiology. Portal hypertension (PH) leads to reduced intestinal motility with bacterial stasis and overgrowth in addition to impaired gastrointestinal immunity. PH also causes gut wall edema; this confluence of factors can predispose to translocation of bacteria from the gut lumen into the bloodstream or across the wall into the peritoneal cavity. These pathogens can seed the peritoneal cavity, which, in patients with ascites, provides a perfect growth-medium for bacteria. Symptoms can include fever, hepatic encephalopathy, abdominal pain, and signs and symptoms of sepsis. The risk is higher in patients with lower serum albumin concentrations and in those who have experienced prior episodes of SBP. Diagnosis is made by diagnostic paracentesis that show an absolute neutrophil count of at least 250 cells/mm3, which is present in this case. Gram stain is not sensitive for the diagnosis, but common pathogens include enteric flora, Escherichia coli, Streptococcus spp, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Treatment is with antibiotics, usually a third-generation cephalosporin, followed by prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Alcoholic hepatitis (Choice A) classically presents with fever, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly in a patient with active alcohol use. An increase in aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase in a ratio of greater than 2:1 is also typical, but this diagnosis should only be made after SBP and other sources of fever have been excluded.

Carcinomatosis (Choice B) refers to metastatic disease involving the peritoneum and is frequently encountered in certain gynecologic cancers, such as ovarian cancer, or in primary peritoneal mesothelioma. Ascites formation occurs as a result of lymphatic obstruction, and tumor cells are often present in the ascitic fluid. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with SBP.

Enteric perforation (Choice C) would be expected to lead to severe sepsis and clinical examination findings of peritonitis. Mild tenderness and shifting dullness are more consistent with SBP, and the patient is unlikely to have a perforation without significant peritoneal signs.

Peritoneal tuberculosis (Choice D) is a rare cause of ascites in the United States. It is more common in patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection or in those who have emigrated from endemic areas. Ascitic fluid analysis typically shows a lymphocytic predominance, and the patient is unlikely to have a perforation without significant peritoneal signs.

questionStem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain and a decreased energy level. The first episode of abdominal pain occurred after he ate a large meal. He then had an urgent need to move his bowels and passed watery stool containing bright red blood. At first, subsequent episodes occurred once or twice weekly and only involved abdominal pain. Four weeks ago, he started to have daily pain associated with bloody, watery stools. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He visited Mexico 1 year ago. He is sexually active with one male partner, and they do not use condoms consistently. He appears pale and tired. He is 191 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 83 kg (183 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is scaphoid with mild, diffuse tenderness. No masses are palpated. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, Hematocrit 29%, Leukocyte count 7800/mm3, Platelet count 310,000/mm3, Serum Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody positive, Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody negative. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows pseudopolyps and inflamed, friable mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is the most likely diagnosis in this young patient with chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, hematochezia, and colonoscopy showing friable mucosa and pseudopolyps. UC is a chronic inflammatory condition within the spectrum of inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulcers of the colonic mucosa, typically beginning with the rectum and advancing proximally. Symptoms range in severity from mild to severe and may include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. Colonoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and demonstrates inflamed mucosa and ulcerations, sometimes in association with inflammatory pseudopolyps, extending in a continuous fashion proximally from the rectum. The presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and a negative test for antibodies to Saccharomyces cerevisiae further support the diagnosis of UC.

questionStem: Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows pseudopolyps and inflamed, friable mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) and a negative test for antibodies to Saccharomyces cerevisiae strongly argues for a diagnosis of UC instead of Crohn disease. Treatment depends upon the severity of symptoms and the extent of disease. Mild disease involving only the rectum can often be managed solely with the use of 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) enemas while extensive disease usually requires oral 5-ASA medications or immunomodulating agents, steroids, or biologics.
incorrectExplanation:
Amebic dysentery (Choice A) is usually caused by Entamoeba histolytica and presents with subacute onset of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. Stool polymerase chain reaction, microscopy, or antigen testing can all be used to make the diagnosis. Colonoscopy showing continuous ulceration starting at the rectum in association with a positive ANCA would be an unusual presentation.

Crohn disease (Choice B) involving the colon is sometimes difficult to distinguish from UC, but patients with Crohn disease usually demonstrate transmural inflammation, involvement of the small bowel, and may also have perianal fistulous disease. A positive ANCA and negative S. cerevisiae antibody test are atypical for Crohn disease.

Cytomegalovirus proctitis (Choice C) is an opportunistic infection commonly occurring in immunocompromised patients in the setting of solid-organ or allogeneic stem cell transplantation, severe ulcerative colitis, or AIDS. It presents with abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, watery or bloody diarrhea.

Yersinia enterocolitis (Choice E) is a bacterial infection causing enterocolitis and mesenteric adenitis. It presents with fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, which may be bloody. It is more common in children and is associated with exposure to contaminated food or water.

questionStem: A 55-year-old woman has had vague pain in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen for 4 months and foul-smelling urine for 2 weeks. She appears thin. There is mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen. Rectal examination shows tenderness with no masses. Hematocrit is 29%. Urinalysis shows 50–100 WBC/hpf and 4+ bacteria. Urine culture grows greater than 100,000 colonies/mL of mixed fecal flora. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Colon cancer is the most likely cause of this patient’s foul-smelling urine growing fecal bacteria and positive test for occult blood in the stool. Colon cancer is the third most common cancer in adults and most often presents after the age of 50 years, although patients with hereditary disorders or a positive family history of colon cancer frequently develop cancer at a younger age. Colorectal cancer is one of the few malignancies for which routine screening using colonoscopy can meaningfully change outcomes, as lesions that are detected early are often curable, while patients who present with symptoms referable either to the primary tumor or to metastatic disease have a far worse prognosis. In the case of this patient, the presence of fecal flora in the urine suggests a colovesical or other gastrointestinal-urinary fistula, which likely developed following erosion of a primary colonic mass into the bladder. The concomitant presence of a positive fecal occult blood stool test lends further evidence to the presence of a colonic mass, while her thin appearance, the duration of her symptoms, and a hematocrit of 29% suggest that the tumor has been present for at least 4 months and likely much longer. The next step in her evaluation should include a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast and a colonoscopy. Treatment is largely determined by the extent of disease.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Amebiasis (Choice A) is usually caused by Entamoeba histolytica and presents with subacute onset of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. Stool polymerase chain reaction, microscopy, or antigen testing can all be used to make the diagnosis. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with this diagnosis.

Familial polyposis (Choice C) is a genetic syndrome that causes colon cancer in almost 100% of patients if a colectomy is not performed prophylactically. Patients usually present in their 30s or 40s and frequently have a family history of colon cancer. This patient’s colon cancer is more likely sporadic given her age and lack of family history.

questionStem: A 68-year-old man has had an enlarging lump under his tongue over the past 3 months. The lesion is now ulcerated and somewhat painful. He quit smoking cigarettes 10 years ago. There is a mass adjacent to the inferior dental arch extending to the inferior surface of the tongue. Submental lymph nodes are palpable, but there is no neck adenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Wide excision of the mass with radical neck dissection

correctExplanation: Oropharyngeal carcinoma is common and may occur in the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, or nasal cavity. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of oropharyngeal carcinoma and is strongly associated with tobacco use and infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). Patients may present with an oropharyngeal lump or nodule, non-healing ulcer, dysphagia, odynophagia, and weight loss. Establishing the diagnosis with a biopsy is essential to guiding further management. Staging can be aided by cervical sentinel lymph node biopsy and imaging with CT or MRI scanning. Early-stage disease may be managed successfully with surgical excision, although more advanced lesions usually require a combined approach with surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: Panoramic x-ray of the jaw (Choice A) is not useful for characterizing soft tissue tumors of the oropharyngeal cavity. Bone involvement is rare in oropharyngeal carcinoma and usually only occurs with large or advanced lesions. Barium swallow (Choice B) is not useful for the diagnosis of oropharyngeal carcinoma. Biopsy is the most important initial step. Biopsy of the lymph nodes (Choice D) is useful for staging of oropharyngeal carcinoma but is not as useful for establishing the initial diagnosis. Biopsy of the primary, sublingual lesion should be performed prior to lymph node biopsy. Wide excision of the mass with radical neck dissection (Choice E) involves removal of the primary lesion as well as involved cervical lymph nodes, internal jugular vein, sternocleidomastoid, spinal accessory nerve, and parotid and submandibular glands. This procedure reduces the risk of further metastatic spread and may be appropriate for advanced lesions.

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician due to a 3-month history of a sore throat and difficulty swallowing. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and drinks alcohol occasionally. Physical examination shows a 2-cm ulcerated lesion on the right tonsil. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questionStem: A 67-year-old man remains intubated and mechanically ventilated 6 hours after admission to the hospital for hematemesis. He has alcoholic cirrhosis and was brought to the emergency department 6 hours after he vomited a copious amount of blood. He has received 4 units of packed red blood cells. His current temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 105/min, and blood pressure is 130/75 mm Hg. Examination shows peripheral muscle wasting. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The abdomen is moderately distended and nontender. There is no fluid wave. His hematocrit is 29%. Placement of a nasogastric tube yields dark blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cirrhosis can be complicated by portal hypertension, which often leads to the development of esophageal or gastric varices that may rupture and lead to massive, life-threatening hematemesis. Additionally, alcoholic gastritis independent of cirrhosis and portal hypertension is a common source of gastrointestinal bleeding. In cirrhosis, obliteration of the hepatic sinusoids through progressive fibrosis increases the resistance to blood flow through the liver, which is transmitted to the portal venous system causing portal hypertension. When engorged secondary to portal hypertension, esophageal veins can be visualized on esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) as vertical dilations underneath the esophageal mucosa, representing dilated submucosal veins (termed ‘varices’). Varices are usually treated endoscopically by band ligation, and patients with cirrhosis must be screened for them, as the risk of life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding is high. The definitive emergent treatment for any source of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is EGD, as it permits both identification of (and sometimes biopsy of) the source (diagnostic) and intervention to control bleeding (therapeutic). This patient presents with hematemesis likely from a ruptured varix, gastritis, or similar upper gastrointestinal source.
incorrectExplanation: Radiolabeled erythrocyte scan (Choice A) can be used in the diagnosis of gastrointestinal bleeding to evaluate for a site of bleeding that is occult or could not be visualized by endoscopy. In this case, the patient is likely experiencing upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which can be diagnosed with upper endoscopy. Mesenteric arteriography (Choice B) would be helpful in cases of gastrointestinal bleeding in the small or lower bowel. While not as sensitive as a radiolabeled erythrocyte scan, it permits direct visualization of contrast extravasation at the site of bleeding, which allows for definitive intervention via coil embolization.

questionStem: A 77-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of difficulty swallowing solids and liquids associated with gurgling in his throat. During this period, he has been waking during the night because of coughing and has had bad breath. He has not had any other symptoms. He underwent appendectomy at the age of 25 years and cholecystectomy for gallstones at the age of 50 years. He currently takes no medications. Examination today shows no abnormalities except for halitosis. A barium swallow is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Therapy with a proton pump inhibitor

correctExplanation: A Zenker diverticulum occurs within the hypopharynx between the cricopharyngeus muscle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle. The mechanism of formation includes an uncoordinated swallowing mechanism, which results in muscle spasms of the cricopharyngeus leading to pulsion diverticula as the wall of the hypopharynx and superior esophagus weakens. Symptoms include halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and dysphagia. Barium swallow reveals a posterior, midline outpouching above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus. Treatment includes surgical repair and resection (diverticulectomy), as well as dietary modifications to include soft or liquid foods.
incorrectExplanation: Dietary counseling (Choice A) is a component of the management of Zenker diverticulum but is secondary to definitive treatment with diverticulectomy.

questionStem: A 16-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after they noticed a small amount of bright red blood in his diaper 2 hours ago. The boy awakened twice overnight screaming as if in pain, and the parents first saw the blood after the second awakening. The patient ate well and was playing normally prior to going to bed. Ten days ago, he had an upper respiratory tract infection which resolved without treatment. On arrival, the child is sleeping and is difficult to arouse. Vital signs are within normal limits. Palpation of the abdomen discloses mild tenderness and a mobile, 4 × 3-cm mass. There is no distention, rebound, or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. A small amount of blood and mucus is noted in the patient's diaper. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An abdominal x-ray series shows a nonspecific gas pattern. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Upper gastrointestinal series with small bowel follow-through

correctExplanation: Intussusception refers to the telescoping of a portion of the intestine into itself, most commonly at the ileocolic junction. Symptoms include severe, intermittent abdominal pain, emesis, and hematochezia. Young children may be observed drawing their legs up toward their abdomen during pain episodes, and physical examination may disclose a palpable abdominal mass, as in this patient. Intussusception can be idiopathic or occur at a lead point, such as an area of inflammation or Meckel diverticulum. The intussusception leads to venous congestion, which results in intestinal edema with subsequent ischemia and necrosis. Severe cases lead to intestinal perforation and peritonitis. It most commonly occurs in children less than 2 years of age and is often preceded by a viral infection. Diagnosis is typically made with ultrasonography, which can disclose a “target sign” at the point of intussusception. Ultrasonography can also be used in conjunction with an air enema as both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure pair for intussusception that has not progressed to perforation.

A CT scan can identify the area of intussusception but exposes the child to large amounts of radiation and does not reduce the intussusception. Laparotomy (Choice C) is not yet indicated in this patient. Laparotomy is a surgical intervention reserved for severe cases of intussusception that evolve to bowel necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis. Bowel perforation and peritonitis are surgical emergencies and often present with fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and severe abdominal pain with rebound and guarding.

questionStem: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of increasing abdominal distention and left lower quadrant tenderness. The patient has a history of Parkinson disease and chronic constipation. Medications are carbidopa-levodopa and docusate and enemas as needed. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is distended and moderately tender to palpation over the left lower quadrant; no peritoneal tenderness, masses, or hernias are noted. Results of laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm³. An abdominal x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Sigmoid volvulus is the most likely cause of this patient’s abdominal distention and pain. The x-ray of the abdomen discloses a grossly distended, air-filled colon with a dense, vertically oriented line that represents two walls of the colon in apposition (coffee-bean sign). Various other x-ray features, including the Frimann-Dahl sign, the presence of a distended colonic loop over the liver (liver overlap sign), and the absence of rectal gas, are useful in supporting this diagnosis. A sigmoid volvulus results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery, which can lead to large bowel obstruction and perforation or intestinal necrosis if not appropriately treated. Patients commonly present with symptoms secondary to a large bowel obstruction, such as constipation, abdominal bloating, distention, nausea, and vomiting. In patients without complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation, treatment requires detorsion of the sigmoid colon and mesentery through sigmoidoscopy with placement of a rectal tube to facilitate stool passage and maintain decompression. Recurrent sigmoid volvulus may require surgical colopexy or sigmoid colectomy.

She has been exclusively fed with a cow milk-based formula. She appears pale and lethargic. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotic therapy, bowel rest with fluid replacement, gastric decompression, and serial abdominal examinations. A common physical examination sign is the squirt sign, which is an elimination of gas and stool following a digital rectal examination. questionStem: A 47-year-old homeless woman with alcoholism is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark maroon fluid three times during the past 6 hours. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. There is dark, crusted vomitus around her mouth, and scleral icterus. Abdominal examination shows ascites. Mental status examination shows short-term memory loss; she is oriented to person and place but not to time. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 7 g/dL, Leukocyte count 12,000/mm³, Serum Total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, Direct 3.5 mg/dL. Administration of fluids is begun. Upper endoscopy shows esophageal varices with evidence of recent bleeding; no other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Operative creation of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt
choices.D: Placement of a transjugular portosystemic stent

correctExplanation: Variceal bleeding is a major cause of mortality in patients with cirrhosis, as patients can suffer large volume hemorrhage in a short period of time. In addition to volume resuscitation, transfusion of blood products, and airway protection, emergent upper esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is required to achieve hemostasis. Endoscopic interventions are the definitive treatment for active variceal hemorrhage. The two most common methods are variceal banding (also called variceal ligation) and sclerotherapy. Banding involves placement of small elastic bands to ligate the bleeding vessel. Sclerotherapy involves injection of a sclerosing solution in the vicinity of the vessel. Risk factors for variceal bleeding include the varix size, anatomical appearance, coagulopathy, and severity of cirrhosis. Additionally, patients with variceal bleeding in the setting of cirrhosis have improved outcomes with administration of somatostatin analogues (octreotide), antibiotics, and proton pump inhibitors.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

questionStem: A 54-year-old man with a history of cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department due to hematemesis. He has had several episodes of vomiting bright red blood over the past 2 hours. His blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. He is lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool extremities and dry mucous membranes. There is abdominal distension with shifting dullness. After initial resuscitation with intravenous fluids and packed red blood cells, the patient undergoes upper endoscopy, which reveals large esophageal varices with active bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Operative creation of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt
choices.D: Placement of a transjugular portosystemic stent

incorrectExplanation: Intravenous administration of ADH (vasopressin) (Choice A) is a pharmacologic adjunct that can be employed to decrease portal venous pressure and reduce mortality from variceal bleeding. In the setting of a variceal bleed, TIPS is reserved as a rescue therapy if endoscopic interventions fail or if there is recurrent bleeding. Extrahepatic placement of a transjugular portosystemic stent (Choice D) is not commonly performed. Placement of a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (Choice C), also called balloon tamponade, is reserved for temporary stabilization of patients with life-threatening bleeding until definitive treatment can be achieved. Balloon tamponade has a high complication and rebleeding rate and places the patient at risk of lethal esophageal rupture. It is generally reserved for use only in cases of failure of less morbid measures.

questionStem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. She has had similar episodes in the past, but they resolved spontaneously. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination shows marked tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Abdominal ultrasonography is the first-line diagnostic examination for the evaluation of potential acute cholecystitis. Acute cholecystitis occurs secondary to obstruction of the cystic duct from a gallstone, which results in subsequent inflammation of the gallbladder wall. It typically presents with fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation, often in a patient with a history of gallstones. It is occasionally preceded by symptoms of biliary colic from cholelithiasis. Characteristic ultrasonography findings of acute cholecystitis include gallbladder wall thickening and hyperemia, pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstones, dilated biliary ducts, and a sonographic Murphy sign (pain with compression directly over the gallbladder). If ultrasonography findings are equivocal, a HIDA scan, a nuclear medicine scan that evaluates for patency of the cystic duct and biliary tree, can be performed. Treatment includes supportive therapy, intravenous fluids, intravenous antibiotics, and urgent cholecystectomy.

Upper gastrointestinal (GI) series (Choice B) is a fluoroscopic examination utilized for evaluation of the upper GI tract to investigate diseases such as peptic ulcer disease, gastric or duodenal neoplasms, malrotation or malformation, and complications following upper GI surgery such as gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. It is not helpful in evaluating the gallbladder or biliary tree. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) (Choice C) evaluates the anatomy and patency of the biliary tree through endoscopic canalization of the duodenal ampulla. ERCP is indicated in the evaluation of acute and chronic biliary pathology, where it serves both a diagnostic and therapeutic purpose, including in the management of acute cholangitis, choledocholithiasis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis.
